title: 6  Polynomial interpolation
text:
6.5 Extra exercises

Exercise 6.4 
Consider \(f(x) = e^{-x}\) on \([-1,1]\).

Find a Lagrange interpolating polynomial \(p\) of \(f\) on \(\{ -1, 0 , 1\}\),
Write down an error estimate for approximating \(f\) with \(p\) on \([-1,1]\).


1. With \(x_0=-1, x_1=0, x_2=1\) and \(f(x_0)=e, f(x_1)=1, f(x_2)=e^{-1}\), the Lagrange polynomials are
\[\begin{align}
\ell_0(x) &= \frac{x(x-1)}{2}, \nonumber\\
%
\ell_1(x) &= 1-x^2, \nonumber\\
%
\ell_2(x) &= \frac{x(x+1)}{2},
\end{align}\]
so
\[\begin{align}
p(x) &= e\,\frac{x(x-1)}{2} + (1-x^2) + e^{-1}\frac{x(x+1)}{2} \nonumber\\
    &= \left(\frac{e+e^{-1}}{2}-1\right)x^2 - \frac{e-e^{-1}}{2}\,x + 1.
\end{align}\]

Here \(n=2\) and \(f^{(3)}(x) = -e^{-x}\), so \(\max_{[-1,1]}|f^{(3)}| = e\). The node polynomial is \(\ell_X(x) = (x+1)x(x-1) = x^3-x\); it vanishes at \(\pm1\) and its critical points are \(x=\pm1/\sqrt3\), where \(|x^3-x| = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(1-\frac13\right) = \frac{2}{3\sqrt3}\). By Theorem 6.2,

\[\begin{align}
|f(x)-p(x)| &\leq \frac{e}{3!}\,|x^3-x| \nonumber\\
%
&\leq \frac{e}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}
\nonumber\\
%
&= \frac{e}{9\sqrt3} \;\approx\; 0.174
\end{align}\]
for all \(x\in [-1,1]\).
(The actual maximum error is about \(0.079\).)



Exercise 6.5 (Growth of the equispaced node polynomial) 
Let \(X = \{x_0 < \cdots < x_n\}\) be \(n+1\) equispaced nodes on \([-1,1]\), i.e. \(x_j = -1 + jh\) with \(h = 2/n\), and let \(\ell_X(x) = (x-x_0)(x-x_1)\cdots(x-x_n)\) be the node polynomial.

Fix \(x \in [x_k, x_{k+1}]\) for some \(0 \leq k \leq n-1\). By bounding \(|x - x_j|\) for \(j < k\) and \(j > k+1\) and using \(|x-x_k|\,|x-x_{k+1}| \leq h^2/4\), show that
\[
    |\ell_X(x)| \leq \frac{h^{n+1}}{4} (k+1)!\,(n-k)!,
\]
and deduce that \(\max_{x\in[-1,1]} |\ell_X(x)| \leq \dfrac{n!}{4} h^{n+1}\).
Use Stirling’s formula, \(n! \sim \sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n\), to show that there is a constant \(C > 0\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
    \max_{x\in[-1,1]} |\ell_X(x)| \leq C\, \frac{(2/e)^n}{\sqrt n} \qquad \text{for all } n.
\]
By evaluating \(\ell_X\) at the point \(x^* = x_0 + h/2\), show that there is a constant \(c > 0\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
    \max_{x\in[-1,1]} |\ell_X(x)| \geq c\, \frac{(2/e)^n}{n} \qquad \text{for all } n.
\]

Note that \(2/e \approx 0.736\): parts 2 and 3 together show that \(\max\limits_{x\in[-1,1]} |\ell_X(x)|\) decays exponentially, but at a rate no better than \((2/e)^n\).

◆

This exercise is more difficult




Exercise 6.6 (A convergence threshold for Runge’s example) 
Fix \(\alpha > 0\) and let \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+\alpha x^2}\), as in Example 6.2 (with \(\alpha=25\)).

Using the geometric series \(f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (-\alpha)^k x^{2k}\) for \(|x| < 1/\sqrt\alpha\), show that
\[\begin{align}
    f^{(2k)}(0) &= (2k)!\,(-\alpha)^k, \nonumber\\
    f^{(2k+1)}(0) &= 0. \nonumber
\end{align}\]
Using partial fractions (the poles of \(f\) are at \(x = \pm i/\sqrt\alpha\)), show more generally that
\[
    \max_{x \in [-1,1]} |f^{(n)}(x)| = n!\, \alpha^{n/2},
\]
with the maximum attained at \(x=0\).
Combine part 2 with Exercise 6.5 and Theorem 6.2 to show that, for \(X\) the equispaced nodes on \([-1,1]\),
\[
    |f(x) - I_Xf(x)| \leq C\sqrt\alpha \, \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \left( \frac{2\sqrt\alpha}{e} \right)^n,
\]
and deduce that this bound converges to \(0\) whenever \(\alpha < \frac{e^2}{4} \approx 1.847\).

It turns out that we have convergence for all \(\alpha < \alpha_{\rm c} \approx 3.621\) Trefethen (2019), Epperson (1987).
Next week, we will see that for Chebyshev nodes, the node polynomial instead satisfies \(|\ell_X(x)| \leq 2^{1-n}\) and so
\[
    |f(x) - I_Xf(x)| \leq 2\sqrt\alpha \left( \frac{\sqrt\alpha}{2} \right)^n,
\]
which converges to \(0\) whenever \(\alpha < 4\). (A sharper argument, using that \(f\) is analytic throughout a neighbourhood of \([-1,1]\) in \(\mathbb C\) rather than just bounding derivatives along the real axis shows that Chebyshev interpolation converges for all \(\alpha > 0\).)

title: 7  Chebyshev polynomials
text:
7.2 How to choose \(X\) to minimise \(\| \ell_X \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])}\)?
In this section, we will write \(\| f \|_{L^\infty} := \max\limits_{x \in [-1,1]} |f(x)|\).
Recall that
\[\begin{align}
    \left\| f - I_Xf \right\|_{L^\infty} \leq \frac{\|f^{(n+1)}\|_{L^\infty}}{(n+1)!} \|\ell_X\|_{L^\infty}  
\end{align}\]
so it is natural to want to minimise
\[\begin{align}
    \|\ell_X\|_{L^\infty} = \max_{x \in [-1,1]} |(x-x_0)(x-x_1)\dots(x-x_n)|
\end{align}\]
over all choices of \(X = \{x_0,\dots,x_n\}\). Equivalently, we are minimising \(\| p \|_{L^\infty}\) over all monic polynomials \(p\) of degree \(n+1\): that is, over all \(p\) such that \(p(x) = x^{n+1} + q(x)\) with \(q\in \mathcal P_n\). We will show that scaled Chebyshev polynomials (of the first kind) solve this (so-called Chebyshev) problem.

title: 7  Chebyshev polynomials
section: 7.3 A Very Brief Introduction to Chebyshev Polynomials
text:
7.3 A Very Brief Introduction to Chebyshev Polynomials

Definition 7.1 For \(x \in [-1,1]\) there exists \(\theta \in [0,\pi]\) such that \(x = \cos\theta\). We can therefore define \(T_n\) on \([-1,1]\) by the condition that
\[\begin{align}
T_n( \cos \theta ) = \cos n\theta.
\end{align}\]
for \(n = 0,1,2,...\).

We will show that \(T_n\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\). We define \(X_{\mathrm{I}}\) to be the set of \(n+1\) zeros of \(T_{n+1}\) and \(X_{\mathrm{II}}\) to be the set of \(n+1\) extreme points of \(T_n\). We will show that
\[\begin{align}
    X_{\mathrm I} &= \Big\{ \cos \frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2(n+1)} \Big\}_{j=0}^{n} \nonumber\\
    X_{\mathrm{II}} &= \big\{ \cos\tfrac{j\pi}{n} \big\}_{j=0}^n
\end{align}\]
\(X_{\mathrm{I}}\) and \(X_{\mathrm{II}}\) are the Chebyshev nodes of the first and second kind, respectively.

Exercise 7.1 
Show that \(T_0(x) = 1\) and \(T_1(x) = x\).


Exercise 7.2 
Use \(\cos(x+y) = \cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y\) to show that

\(T_{n+1}(x) = 2x T_{n}(x) - T_{n-1}(x)\) for \(n =1,2,\dots\),
Hence show that \(T_n\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\),
Show that the coefficent of \(x^n\) in \(T_n\) is \(2^{n-1}\) for \(n \geq 1\).



Exercise 7.3 
Show that

\(\|T_n\|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} = 1\),
\(T_{n}\big( \cos\tfrac{j\pi}{n} \big) = (-1)^j\) for \(j = 0,\dots,n\) (extreme points; Chebyshev nodes of the second kind),
\(T_{n+1} = 0\) on \(\big\{ \cos \frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2(n+1)} \big\}_{j=0}^{n}\) (zeros; Chebyshev nodes of the first kind).



Proof. Firstly, \(T_0(\cos\theta) =\cos 0 = 1\) and so \(T_0 = 1\). Moreover, \(T_{1}(\cos \theta) = \cos\theta\) and so \(T_1 = x\).
Using the fact that \(\cos(x+y) = \cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y\) (which follows from e.g. \(e^{i(x+y)} = e^{ix} e^{iy}\)), we find that
\[\begin{align}
    T_{n\pm1}(\cos\theta) &= \cos( n\theta \pm \theta) \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \cos \theta \cos n\theta  \mp  \sin\theta \sin n\theta.
\end{align}\]
The sum of these equations is therefore \(T_{n+1}(\cos\theta) + T_{n-1}(\cos\theta) = 2 \cos \theta \cos n\theta = 2 \cos(\theta) T_n(\cos\theta)\) and thus the recursion relation follows.
One can therefore show inductively that \(T_n\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\). Using the recursion, the coeficient of \(x^{n+1}\) in \(T_{n+1}\) is \(2\) times the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(T_{n}\). You can therefore argue inductively that the coeficient of \(x^n\) in \(T_{n}\) is \(2^{n-1}\).
We have \(|T_n(\cos\theta)| = |\cos n\theta| \leq 1\) and this maximum is achieved when \(n\theta = j\pi\) for some \(j \in \mathbb Z\). Restricting this to \(\theta = \frac{j\pi}{n} \in [0,\pi]\) gives \(j = 0,\dots,n\). At these values, we have \(T_n( \cos\tfrac{j\pi}{n} ) = \cos j\pi = (-1)^j\).
\(T_{n+1}\) is a polynomial of degree \(n+1\) and thus has at most \(n+1\) zeros in the interval \([-1,1]\). We have \(T_{n+1}(\cos\theta) = \cos (n+1)\theta = 0\) when \((n+1)\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + j \pi\) for \(j \in \mathbb Z\) such that \(\theta = \frac{ (2j+1) \pi }{ 2(n+1) } \in [0,\pi]\). That is, for \(j = 0,\dots,n\).

Here, we plot the first \(5\) Chebyshev polynomials on \([-1,1]\) together with \((x, T_n(x))\) for \(x \in X_{\mathrm{II}}\) with \(n=5\)


Code
plot(ChebyshevT([1.]), -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)
plot!(ChebyshevT([0, 1]), -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)
plot!(ChebyshevT([0,0,1.]), -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)
plot!(ChebyshevT([0,0,0,1.]), -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)
plot!(ChebyshevT([0,0,0,0,1.]), -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)

p = ChebyshevT([0,0,0,0,0,1.])
plot!(p, -1, 1, title="Chebyshev I", legend = false, lw = 3)

scatter!( @. cos( pi*(0:5)/5 ), @. p( cos( pi* (0:5)/5 ) ) )





We define the monic (with leading coefficient equal to \(1\)) Chebyshev polynomials as \(t_0(x) = 1\) and \(t_n(x) := 2^{1-n} T_n(x)\) for \(n \geq 1\). We are ready for the main result of this lecture:

Theorem 7.1 The monic Chebyshev polynomials solve the Chebyshev problem (on \([-1,1]\)). That is,
\[\begin{align}
    \|t_{n+1} \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} \leq \min_{p = x^{n+1} + q : \,\, q \in \mathcal P_n  } \big\| p \big\|_{L^\infty([-1,1])}.
\end{align}\]


Proof. Here, we just write \(\|\,\cdot\,\|_{L^\infty}\) for \(\|\,\cdot\,\|_{L^\infty([-1,1])}\).
Suppose that \(p\) minimises the right hand side of (1). Then, because \(t_{n+1}\) is a monic polynomial of degree \(n+1\), we must have
\[\begin{align*}
    \big\|p \big\|_{L^\infty} \leq \| t_{n+1} \|_{L^\infty} = 2^{1-(n+1)} \| T_{n+1} \|_{L^\infty} = 2^{-n}
\end{align*}\]
Define \(r(x) = t_{n+1}(x) - p(x)\) and note that
\[\begin{align}
    r( z_j ) = (-1)^j 2^{-n} - p( z_j ), \qquad \text{for } z_j := \cos \frac{j\pi}{n+1}
\end{align}\]
and \(j = 0,1,\dots,n+1\) (here, we have used the fact that \(z_j\) are the extreme values of \(T_{n+1}\) for \(j=0,\dots,n+1\)).
Therefore, since \(|p(x)| \leq 2^{-n}\) for all \(x \in [-1,1]\), we have
\[\begin{align}
    r( z_j ) &= 2^{-n} - p( z_j ) \geq 0 \qquad &\text{for even } j \\
    r( z_j ) &= (-1) 2^{-n} - p( z_j ) \leq 0 \qquad &\text{for odd } j.
\end{align}\]
By the change of sign theorem, there exists \(x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}\) such that \(z_j \leq x_{j+1} \leq z_{j+1}\) and \(r(x_j) = 0\). As a result, \(r\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(n\) with \(n+1\) zeros and thus \(r = 0\) and \(p = t_{n+1}\).

We have therefore shown that, choosing \(X =X_{\mathrm{I}}=  \{ \text{zeros of }t_{n+1} \}\) minimises the node polynomial in the following sense
\[\begin{align}
    \min_{ y_0 < \dots < y_n } \| \ell_{Y} \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} \geq \| \ell_X \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} = 2^{-n}
\end{align}\]
It turns out that \(\ell_{X_{\mathrm{II}}}(x) = 2^{-n} \big( T_{n+1}(x) - T_{n-1}(x) \big)\) and so \(\|\ell_{X_{\mathrm{II}}}\|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} \leq 2^{1-n}\) (here, we used \(|T_{n}|\leq 1\)) and so, in practice, one expects the same approximation rates when using \(X = X_{\mathrm{II}} = \{\text{extreme points of } T_n \}\).

Exercise 7.4 
Recall that \(T_{n+1}(x) = 2x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x)\) for \(n=1,2,...\).

Use the recursion to write down \(T_2\), \(T_3\) and \(T_4\) in the monomial basis.
Write down the Chebyshev nodes of the first kind \(X_{\mathrm I}\) for \(n = 2\) (i.e. the zeros of \(T_3\)) and check directly that \(\ell_{X_{\mathrm I}}(x) = t_3(x) = x^3 - \tfrac34 x\).
Find \(\| \ell_{X_{\mathrm I}} \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])}\) for \(n=2\) by calculus, and compare with the equispaced nodes \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\).



Exercise 7.5 
In the notes, we claimed that \(\ell_{X_{\mathrm{II}}}(x) = 2^{-n} \big( T_{n+1}(x) - T_{n-1}(x) \big)\) for \(n \geq 1\). Since \(\|T_n\|_{L^\infty} = 1\), this gives \(\| \ell_{X_{\rm II}} \|_{L^\infty} \leq 2^{1-n}\).
Prove the claim as follows:

Show that \(T_{n+1}(\cos\theta) - T_{n-1}(\cos\theta) = -2 \sin\theta \sin n\theta\).
Deduce that \(T_{n+1} - T_{n-1}\) vanishes on \(X_{\mathrm{II}} = \big\{ \cos\frac{j\pi}{n} \big\}_{j=0}^n\).
Show that \(2^{-n} \big( T_{n+1} - T_{n-1} \big)\) is monic of degree \(n+1\), and conclude.



Exercise 7.6 
Suppose we want to interpolate on a general interval \([a,b]\) rather than \([-1,1]\).

Let \(\phi(t) = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{b-a}{2} t\), so that \(\phi\) maps \([-1,1]\) onto \([a,b]\). If \(Y = \{y_0,\dots,y_n\} \subset [-1,1]\) and \(X = \phi(Y) = \{\phi(y_0), \dots, \phi(y_n)\}\), show that \[
    \ell_X\big(\phi(t)\big) = \left( \frac{b-a}{2} \right)^{n+1} \ell_Y(t).
\]
Deduce that, if \(X\) is the image of \(X_{\mathrm I}\) under \(\phi\), then \(\max_{x \in [a,b]} |\ell_X(x)| = 2 \left( \frac{b-a}{4} \right)^{n+1}\).
Let \(f(x) = \sin x\) on \([0, \pi]\), interpolated at the image of \(X_{\mathrm I}\). Write down an error bound and find the smallest \(n\) that guarantees \(\max_{x\in[0,\pi]} |f(x) - I_Xf(x)| \leq 10^{-6}\).

title: 8  Barycentric formula and divided differences
text:
8.2 Barycentric formula
See e.g. Berrut and Trefethen (2004) link for more details.

Exercise 8.1 
Let’s use the formula
\[
\begin{align}
    I_Xf(x) &= \sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j) \ell_j(x), \\
    %
    \ell_j(x) &:= \prod_{k\not=j} \frac{x - x_k}{x_j - x_k} \nonumber
\end{align}
\tag{8.1}\]
to compute the polynomial interpolation of \(f(x) = \frac1{1+25x^2}\) (Runge function, as above):


Code
Runge = t -> 1/(1 + 25t^2)

function ℓⱼ( j, t, x ) 
    if j == 0
        return prod( @. t - x[2:end] ) / prod( @. x[1] - x[2:end] )
    elseif j == length(x)-1 
        return prod( @. t - x[1:end-1] ) / prod( @. x[end] - x[1:end-1] )
    else
        return prod( @. t - x[1:j] ) * prod( @. t - x[(j+2):end] ) / ( prod( @. x[j+1] - x[1:j] ) * prod( @. x[j+1] - x[(j+2):end] ) )
    end
end 

function p_naive( t, x, y ) 
    r = 0
    for j in 0:(length(x)-1)
        r = r + ℓⱼ(j, t, x) * y[j+1] 
    end
    return r
end 

egrid = range(-1, 1, length=401)

anim = @animate for n ∈ [10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 700, 760, 780:20:1020...]
    x = @. cos( π*(0:n)/n )
    y = @. Runge( x )
    p = p_naive.( egrid, Ref(x), Ref(y) )
    err = @. max( abs( p - Runge(egrid) ), 1e-17 )

    plt1 = plot(Runge, -1, 1; label=L"y = f(x)", lw = 3, linestyle = :dash, 
            title = "Naive Lagrange formula: n = $n", ylims = (-0.5, 1.5))
    plot!(plt1, egrid, p; label=L"y = p(x)", lw = 3 )
    scatter!(plt1, x, y; primary = false, markersize = 2, markerstrokewidth = 0)

    plt2 = plot(egrid, err; yscale = :log10, ylims = (1e-17, 1e2), legend = false, lw = 2,
            title = @sprintf("max error = %.2e", maximum(err)))
    plot( plt1, plt2; size=(1000, 500) )
end

gif(anim, "../images/Naive Lagrange.gif", fps = 1, show_msg = false)





What is happening here?

Underflow! The products \(\prod_{k} (t - x_k)\) and \(\prod_{k\not=j} (x_j - x_k)\) are of size roughly \(2^{-n}\) (and the partial products computed in the code can be even smaller). Around \(n \approx 800\), these partial products fall below the smallest normal double (\(\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-308}\)) into the subnormal range, where precision is lost.


Notice also that, in order to compute (8.1), we need \(O(n^2)\) operations (flops) for each \(x\) - so it is slow and unstable!
Instead, we may use the Barycentric formula which we now derive. First notice that
\[
\begin{align}
    \ell_j(x) &= \prod_{k \not= j} \frac{x - x_k}{x_j - x_k}
    \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \lambda_j \frac{\ell_X(x)}{x- x_j}
\end{align}
\tag{8.2}\]
where \(\lambda_j := \frac{1}{ \prod_{k \not= j} (x_j - x_k) }\). As a result, we have
\[
\begin{align}
    I_Xf(x) &= \sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j) \ell_j(x) \nonumber \\
    %
    &= \ell_X(x) \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j f(x_j)}{x- x_j}.
\end{align}
\]
This is sometimes referred to as the first form of the Barycentric formula.

Exercise 8.2 
Suppose that \(X = \{ x_0 < ... < x_n \}\) and let \(\ell_j\) be the corresponding Lagrange polynomials. Show that \(\sum_{j=0}^n \ell_j(x) = 1\) for all \(x\).

Therefore, using (8.2) and dividing by \(\sum_{j=0}^n \ell_j(x) = 1\), we obtain (for \(x \not\in X\))
\[
\begin{align}
    I_Xf(x) &= \left. \sum_{j=0}^n \ell_j(x) f(x_j) \middle/ \sum_{j=0}^n \ell_j(x) \right. \nonumber\\
    &= \left. \ell_X(x) \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j f(x_j)}{x - x_j} \middle/ \ell_X(x) \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j}{x - x_j} \right. \nonumber\\
    &= \left. \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j f(x_j)}{x - x_j} \middle/ \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j}{x - x_j} \right.
\end{align}
\tag{8.3}\]
which is known as the Barycentric formula.
For a fixed interpolation set, one may compute \(\lambda_j\) once and then evaluating \(p(x)\) requires only \(O(n)\) computations.
In fact, for Chebyshev nodes \(X_{\mathrm{II}} = \big\{ \cos \frac{j\pi}{n} \big\}_{j=0}^n\), we have a simple formula for the \(\lambda_j\):
\[
    \lambda_j = \begin{cases}
        \frac{2^{n}}{4n}  & \text{if } j = 0 \\
        (-1)^j \frac{2^{n}}{2n} & \text{if } j = 1,\dots,n-1 \\
        (-1)^n \frac{2^{n}}{4n} & \text{if } j = n
    \end{cases}
\tag{8.4}\]

Exercise 8.3 
Explain why one may instead consider any weights of the form \(w_j := C \lambda_j\) in the Barycentric formula (8.3). Why might this be a good idea? See (8.4) for the weights appearing in the Barycentric formula for Chebyshev nodes of the second kind.

In particular, for Chebyshev nodes of the second kind, we can use (8.3) with the weights \(w_j := (-1)^j \tau_j\) where \(\tau_j = \frac12\) for \(j=0, n\) and \(\tau_j = 1\) otherwise. Moreover, this formula has been proved to be numerically stable (Higham (2004)) which we demonstrate in the following:


Code
# Barycentric formula for Chebyshev nodes of the second kind:
function ChebyshevInterpolant( f, n )
    x = @. cos( π*(0:n)/n )
    y = @. f( x )
    λ = @. (-1.0)^(0:n)
    λ[1] /= 2
    λ[end] /= 2

    return function ( t )
        num = 0.0
        den = 0.0
        for j ∈ 1:(n+1)
            if t == x[j]
                return y[j]
            end
            num += λ[j] * y[j] / (t - x[j])
            den += λ[j] / (t - x[j])
        end
        return num / den
    end
end

egrid = range(-1, 1, length=401)

anim = @animate for n ∈ [10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 700, 760, 780:20:1020..., 1500, 2000, 5000, 10000]
    x = @. cos( π*(0:n)/n )
    p = ChebyshevInterpolant( Runge, n ).( egrid )
    err = @. max( abs( p - Runge(egrid) ), 1e-17 )

    plt1 = plot(Runge, -1, 1; label=L"y = f(x)", lw = 3, linestyle = :dash, 
            title = "Barycentric formula: n = $n", ylims = (-0.5, 1.5))
    plot!(plt1, egrid, p; label=L"y = p(x)", lw = 3 )
    scatter!(plt1, x, Runge.(x); primary = false, markersize = 2, markerstrokewidth = 0)

    plt2 = plot(egrid, err; yscale = :log10, ylims = (1e-17, 1e2), legend = false, lw = 2,
            title = @sprintf("max error = %.2e", maximum(err)))
    plot( plt1, plt2; size=(1000, 500) )
end

gif(anim, "../images/Barycentric.gif", fps = 1, show_msg = false)






Exercise 8.4 
Recall that the degree \(2\) polynomial interpolation of \(f(x) = \sin x\) on \(X = \{ x_0 < x_1 < x_2 \} = \{ 0, \frac\pi2, \pi \}\) is \(I_X f(x) = -\frac4{\pi^2} x(x-\pi)\). Write the Barycentric version of this formula (8.3).
Explain how you would have to update this formula if we added an extra point \(x_{3} = -2\pi\) to the interpolation set.

The Barycentric formula (8.3) depends on the weights \(\lambda_j = \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j-x_k)^{-1}\) which in this case are given by
\[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_0 &= \frac{1}{(0-\frac\pi2)(0-\pi)} = \frac2{\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_1 &= \frac{1}{(\frac\pi2-0)(\frac\pi2 - \pi)} = -\frac4{\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_2 &= \frac{1}{(\pi - 0)(\pi-\frac\pi2)} = \frac2{\pi^2}
\end{align}
\]
(which makes sense because \(\{ 0, \frac\pi2, \pi \}\) are Chebyshev nodes of the second kind scaled to \([0,\pi]\). The scaling only multiplies all of the weights by a common constant, which cancels in the Barycentric formula. In general, the Chebyshev weights can be chosen to be \(\frac12, -1, 1, -1, \dots, (-1)^{n-1}, \frac{(-1)^n}{2}\).)
Since \(f(x_{j}) = 0\) for \(j=0,2\), we have
\[
\begin{align}
    I_Xf(x) &= \left.\left(
        \frac{\lambda_0 f(x_0)}{x - x_0} + \frac{\lambda_1 f(x_1)}{x - x_1} + \frac{\lambda_2 f(x_2)}{x - x_2}
    \right) \middle/ \left(
        \frac{\lambda_0}{x - x_0} + \frac{\lambda_1}{x - x_1} + \frac{\lambda_2}{x - x_2}
    \right) \right. \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \left.\left(
        \frac{-1}{x - \frac\pi2}
    \right) \middle/ \left(
        \frac{1/2}{x} + \frac{-1}{x - \frac\pi2} + \frac{1/2}{x - \pi}
    \right) \right.
\end{align}
\]
where, in the second line, we have multiplied all of the weights by \(\frac{\pi^2}{4}\) (which does not change the formula) to obtain the weights \(\frac12, -1, \frac12\).
We would have to update \(\lambda_{j}\) by dividing by \(x_{j} - (-2\pi)\) for each \(j=0,1,2\) so we get \(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2 = \frac{1}{\pi^3}, -\frac{8}{5\pi^3}, \frac{2}{3\pi^3}\) and write down
\[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_3 = \frac{1}{(-2\pi-0)(-2\pi-\frac\pi2)(-2\pi-\pi)} = -\frac{1}{15\pi^3}
\end{align}
\]








TipSolution





The Barycentric formula (8.3) depends on the weights \(\lambda_j = \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j-x_k)^{-1}\) which in this case are given by
\[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_0 &= \frac{1}{(0-\frac\pi2)(0-\pi)} = \frac2{\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_1 &= \frac{1}{(\frac\pi2-0)(\frac\pi2 - \pi)} = -\frac4{\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_2 &= \frac{1}{(\pi - 0)(\pi-\frac\pi2)} = \frac2{\pi^2}
\end{align}
\]
(which makes sense because \(\{ 0, \frac\pi2, \pi \}\) are Chebyshev nodes of the second kind scaled to \([0,\pi]\). The scaling only multiplies all of the weights by a common constant, which cancels in the Barycentric formula. In general, the Chebyshev weights can be chosen to be \(\frac12, -1, 1, -1, \dots, (-1)^{n-1}, \frac{(-1)^n}{2}\).)
Since \(f(x_{j}) = 0\) for \(j=0,2\), we have
\[
\begin{align}
    I_Xf(x) &= \left.\left(
        \frac{\lambda_0 f(x_0)}{x - x_0} + \frac{\lambda_1 f(x_1)}{x - x_1} + \frac{\lambda_2 f(x_2)}{x - x_2}
    \right) \middle/ \left(
        \frac{\lambda_0}{x - x_0} + \frac{\lambda_1}{x - x_1} + \frac{\lambda_2}{x - x_2}
    \right) \right. \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \left.\left(
        \frac{-1}{x - \frac\pi2}
    \right) \middle/ \left(
        \frac{1/2}{x} + \frac{-1}{x - \frac\pi2} + \frac{1/2}{x - \pi}
    \right) \right.
\end{align}
\]
where, in the second line, we have multiplied all of the weights by \(\frac{\pi^2}{4}\) (which does not change the formula) to obtain the weights \(\frac12, -1, \frac12\).
We would have to update \(\lambda_{j}\) by dividing by \(x_{j} - (-2\pi)\) for each \(j=0,1,2\) so we get \(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2 = \frac{1}{\pi^3}, -\frac{8}{5\pi^3}, \frac{2}{3\pi^3}\) and write down
\[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_3 = \frac{1}{(-2\pi-0)(-2\pi-\frac\pi2)(-2\pi-\pi)} = -\frac{1}{15\pi^3}
\end{align}
\]
We plot both interpolants (using the Barycentric formula with the weights above):


Code
# Barycentric formula with the weights computed above
function bary( t, x, λ, y )
    i = findfirst( ==(t), x )
    isnothing(i) || return y[i]
    return sum( @. λ * y / (t - x) ) / sum( @. λ / (t - x) )
end

x2 = [0, π/2, π];        λ2 = [2, -4, 2] / π^2
x3 = [0, π/2, π, -2π];   λ3 = [1, -8/5, 2/3, -1/15] / π^3

plot(sin, -2π, 2π; label=L"y = \sin x", lw=2, linestyle=:dash)
plot!(t -> bary(t, x2, λ2, sin.(x2)), -2π, 2π; label=L"y = p_2(x)", lw=3)
plot!(t -> bary(t, x3, λ3, sin.(x3)), -2π, 2π; label=L"y = p_3(x)", lw=3)
scatter!(x3, sin.(x3); markersize=5, primary=false)

title: 8  Barycentric formula and divided differences
text:
8.3 Newton form & divided differences
Fix \(X = \{x_0, x_1, \cdots, x_{n} \}\). Newton polynomials are the node polynomials corresponding to the first nodes in \(X\):
\[
\begin{align}
    \pi_0(x) &= 1 \nonumber\\
    \pi_1(x) &= \ell_{\{x_0\}}(x) = (x - x_0) \nonumber\\
    \pi_2(x) &= \ell_{\{ x_0, x_1 \}}(x) = (x - x_0)(x-x_1) \nonumber\\
    &\vdots \nonumber\\
    \pi_n(x) &= \ell_{\{ x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} \}}(x) = (x-x_0)(x-x_1)\cdots (x-x_{n-1})
\end{align}
\]

Example 8.1 Recall that the Lagrange interpolation of \(f(x) = \sin x\) on \(X = \{ 0, \frac\pi2, \pi \}\) is \(I_Xf(x) = -\frac4{\pi^2} x(x-\pi)\).


Code
f = x->sin(x)

x = [0, pi/2, pi]
y = f.(x)

p = fit(x,y)
plot(f, -2pi, 2pi,  label=L"y = \sin x", lw=2, linestyle=:dash)
plot!( p, xlims=(-2pi,2pi), label=L"y= p(x)", lw=3)
scatter!( x, y, markersize=5, primary=false)





Derive the same result using the Newton basis \(\pi_0 = 1\), \(\pi_1 = x\), and \(\pi_2 = x(x-\tfrac\pi2)\).



Code
q = (2/π)* Polynomial([0,1,]) - (4/pi^2) * Polynomial( [0, -pi/2, 1] )
plot!(q, xlims=(-2pi,2pi), label=L"y=q(x)")







Notice that if \(p\) interpolates \(f\) at \(X = \{x_0,\dots,x_n\}\) and the \(x_j\) are distinct, then
\[
\begin{align}
    p(x) &= a_0 + a_1 (x - x_0) + a_2 (x-x_0)(x-x_1) + \cdots + a_n (x-x_0)(x-x_1) \cdots (x - x_{n-1})\nonumber\\
    %
    &= f(x_0) + \frac{f(x_1) - f(x_0)}{x_1 - x_0} (x-x_0) + a_2 \pi_2(x) + \cdots + a_n \pi_n(x)
\end{align}
\]

Definition 8.1 We define the divided difference \(f[x_{0}, \dots, x_n]\) to be the leading coefficient in the polynomial interpolation \(p\in \mathcal P_n\) of \(f\) on the set of distinct nodes \(X = \{x_0,x_1,\dots, x_n\}\): that is,
\[
\begin{align}
    p(x) = f[x_0,\dots,x_n] x^n + q(x)
\end{align}
\]
where \(q \in \mathcal P_{n-1}\).

We have seen that \(f[x_0] = f(x_0)\) and \(f[x_0,x_1] = \frac{f(x_1) - f(x_0)}{x_1 - x_0}\). (Here, we just solved \(p(x_0) = f(x_0)\) and \(p(x_1) = f(x_1)\)).

Theorem 8.1 The divided difference \(f[x_{0}, \dots, x_n]\) doesn’t depend on the ordering of the interpolation nodes. Moreover, we have linearity: \((f + c g)[x_0,...,x_n] = f[x_0,...,x_n] + c g[x_0,...,x_n]\).


Proof. The polynomial interpolant \(p\in \mathcal P_n\) of \(f\) on \(X\) is independent of the ordering of the nodes.
Moreover, if \(p\) and \(q\) are the polynomial interpolants of \(f\) and \(g\), respectively, then \(p + c q\) is a polynomial interpolant of \(f+ c g\).


Theorem 8.2 Suppose \(X = \{x_0,\cdots,x_n\}\) is a set of \(n+1\) distinct interpolation nodes. Then, we have the recursion
\[
\begin{align}
    f[x_0, \dots, x_n] &= \frac
        {f[x_1, \dots, x_n] - f[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}]}
        {x_n - x_0}.
\end{align}
\]


Proof. Let \(p \in \mathcal P_{n-1}\) be the polynomial interpolation of \(f\) on \(\{x_0,\dots, x_{n-1}\}\) and define \(g(x) := (x-x_{n})f(x)\) and \(q(x) := (x - x_{n}) p(x)\). Then \(q(x_j) = g(x_j)\) for \(j = 0, \dots, n-1\) (because \(p(x_j) = f(x_j)\)) and \(q(x_n) = 0 = g(x_n)\). Since \(q \in \mathcal P_n\), \(q\) is the polynomial interpolation of \(g\) on \(X\). Therefore, the leading coefficient of \(q\) is both \(g[x_0,\dots,x_{n}]\) (because \(q\) interpolates \(g\) on \(X\)) and \(f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]\) (because \(q\) is \((x-x_{n})\) times \(p\)).
That is, we have \(\big( (x - x_n) f \big) [x_0,\dots,x_n] = f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]\). By relabeling the indices (which is allowed because \(f[x_0,\dots,x_n]\) does not depend on the ordering of the interpolation nodes), we also have \(\big( (x - x_0) f \big) [x_0,\dots,x_n] = f[x_1,\dots,x_{n}]\). Therefore, by linearity we have
\[
\begin{align}
    (x_n - x_0) f[x_0,\dots,x_n] &= \big( (x - x_0) f - (x-x_n) f \big) [x_0,\dots,x_n] \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \big( (x - x_0) f \big) [x_0,\dots,x_n] - \big( (x-x_n) f \big) [x_0,\dots,x_n] \nonumber\\
    %
    &= f [x_1,\dots,x_n] - f [x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}] \nonumber
\end{align}
\]


8.3.1 Divided difference table
Using Theorem 8.2, we can compute all of the divided differences of \(f\) on \(X = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}\) column by column in a divided difference table. For example, when \(n = 3\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
    x_j & f(x_j) & \text{1st} & \text{2nd} & \text{3rd} \\ \hline
    x_0 & f[x_0] & & & \\
        & & f[x_0,x_1] & & \\
    x_1 & f[x_1] & & f[x_0,x_1,x_2] & \\
        & & f[x_1,x_2] & & f[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3] \\
    x_2 & f[x_2] & & f[x_1,x_2,x_3] & \\
        & & f[x_2,x_3] & & \\
    x_3 & f[x_3] & & &
\end{array}
\]
Starting from the values \(f[x_j] = f(x_j)\), each new entry is the difference of its two neighbours in the previous column divided by the difference of the first and last nodes involved:
\[
    f[x_j, \dots, x_{j+k}] = \frac{f[x_{j+1}, \dots, x_{j+k}] - f[x_j, \dots, x_{j+k-1}]}{x_{j+k} - x_j}.
\]
Computing the whole table requires \(O(n^2)\) operations. Adding a new node \(x_{n+1}\) only adds a new row at the bottom of the table (one new entry in each column), which costs \(O(n)\) operations.
The entries along the top diagonal of the table are exactly the coefficients of the Newton form of the polynomial interpolation:

Theorem 8.3 Suppose \(X = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}\) is a set of \(n+1\) distinct interpolation nodes. Then,
\[
    I_X f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n f[x_0, \dots, x_k] \, \pi_k(x).
\]


Proof. Let \(p_k \in \mathcal P_k\) be the polynomial interpolation of \(f\) on \(\{x_0, \dots, x_k\}\). For \(k \geq 1\), \(p_k - p_{k-1} \in \mathcal P_k\) vanishes at \(x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}\), and so \(p_k - p_{k-1} = c_k \pi_k\) for some constant \(c_k\). Since \(p_{k-1} \in \mathcal P_{k-1}\), comparing the coefficients of \(x^k\) gives \(c_k = f[x_0, \dots, x_k]\). Moreover, \(p_0 = f(x_0) = f[x_0] \pi_0\). Therefore, \(I_X f = p_n = p_0 + \sum_{k=1}^n (p_k - p_{k-1}) = \sum_{k=0}^n f[x_0,\dots,x_k] \pi_k\).


Example 8.2 Let’s go back to interpolating \(f(x) =\sin x\) on \(\{0, \frac\pi2, \pi\}\). Now add \(-2\pi\) as an interpolation node and compute the new polynomial interpolant.
We compute the divided difference table with \(x_0 = 0\), \(x_1 = \frac\pi2\), \(x_2 = \pi\), and \(x_3 = -2\pi\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
    x_j & f(x_j) & \text{1st} & \text{2nd} & \text{3rd} \\ \hline
    0 & 0 & & & \\
      & & \frac{2}{\pi} & & \\
    \frac{\pi}{2} & 1 & & -\frac{4}{\pi^2} & \\
      & & -\frac{2}{\pi} & & -\frac{8}{5\pi^3} \\
    \pi & 0 & & -\frac{4}{5\pi^2} & \\
      & & 0 & & \\
    -2\pi & 0 & & &
\end{array}
\]
where the entries are computed using Theorem 8.2:
\[
\begin{align}
    f[x_0,x_1] &= \frac{1 - 0}{\frac\pi2 - 0} = \frac{2}{\pi}, \nonumber\\
    f[x_1,x_2] &= \frac{0 - 1}{\pi - \frac\pi2} = -\frac{2}{\pi}, \nonumber\\
    f[x_2,x_3] &= \frac{0 - 0}{-2\pi - \pi} = 0, \nonumber\\
    f[x_0,x_1,x_2] &= \frac{-\frac2\pi - \frac2\pi}{\pi - 0} = -\frac{4}{\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    f[x_1,x_2,x_3] &= \frac{0 - \big(-\frac2\pi\big)}{-2\pi - \frac\pi2} = -\frac{4}{5\pi^2}, \nonumber\\
    f[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3] &= \frac{-\frac{4}{5\pi^2} - \big(-\frac{4}{\pi^2}\big)}{-2\pi - 0} = -\frac{8}{5\pi^3}. \nonumber
\end{align}
\]
By Theorem 8.3, the coefficients of the Newton form are the entries along the top diagonal of the table, and so
\[
\begin{align}
    p(x) &= 0 + \frac{2}{\pi} x - \frac{4}{\pi^2} x \big(x - \tfrac\pi2\big) \nonumber\\
    &\qquad - \frac{8}{5\pi^3} x\big(x - \tfrac\pi2\big)\big(x - \pi\big). \nonumber
\end{align}
\]
Notice that the first three terms are exactly the interpolant from Example 8.1: adding a node only adds one new term to the Newton form.
We plot this:


Code
r = x-> - 4*x*(x-pi)/pi^2 - 8*x*(x-pi/2)*(x-pi)/(5*pi^3)

x = [0, pi/2, pi, -2pi]
y = f.(x)

plot(f, -2pi, 2pi,  label=L"y = \sin x", lw=2, linestyle=:dash)
plot!( p, xlims=(-2pi,2pi), label=L"y= p_2(x)", lw=3)
plot!( r, xlims=(-2pi,2pi), label=L"y= p_3(x)", lw=3)
scatter!( x, y, markersize=5, primary=false)

8.5 Extra exercises

Exercise 8.5 
Let \(n = 2\) and let \(X = X_{\mathrm{II}} = \big\{ \cos\frac{j\pi}{2} \big\}_{j=0}^2\) be the Chebyshev nodes of the second kind, so that \(x_0 = 1\), \(x_1 = 0\), and \(x_2 = -1\). Compute \(\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2\) directly from the definition \(\lambda_j = \big( \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j - x_k) \big)^{-1}\) and check that they agree with (8.4).

We have \[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_0 &= \frac{1}{(1 - 0)(1 - (-1))} = \frac12, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_1 &= \frac{1}{(0 - 1)(0 - (-1))} = -1, \nonumber\\
    \lambda_2 &= \frac{1}{(-1 - 1)(-1 - 0)} = \frac12. \nonumber
\end{align}
\] With \(n = 2\), (8.4) gives \(\lambda_0 = \frac{2^2}{8} = \frac12\), \(\lambda_1 = (-1)^1 \frac{2^2}{4} = -1\), and \(\lambda_2 = (-1)^2 \frac{2^2}{8} = \frac12\).



Exercise 8.6 
In the notes, we claimed that for the Chebyshev nodes \(X_{\mathrm{II}} = \big\{ x_j = \cos\frac{j\pi}{n} \big\}_{j=0}^n\) the barycentric weights \(\lambda_j := \big( \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j - x_k) \big)^{-1}\) are given by
\[
    \lambda_j = \begin{cases}
        \frac{2^{n}}{4n}  & \text{if } j = 0 \\
        (-1)^j \frac{2^{n}}{2n} & \text{if } j = 1,\dots,n-1 \\
        (-1)^n \frac{2^{n}}{4n} & \text{if } j = n
    \end{cases}
\]
Prove the claim as follows:

Show that \(\lambda_j = 1 / \ell_X'(x_j)\), where \(\ell_X(x) = \prod_{k=0}^n (x - x_k)\) is the node polynomial.
Show that \(T_n'(\cos\theta) = n \frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}\). Using Exercise 7.5, deduce that \[
\ell_X(x) = \frac{2^{1-n}}{n} (x^2 - 1) T_n'(x).
\]
By differentiating \(T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos n\theta\) twice, show that \(T_n\) satisfies the Chebyshev differential equation \[
(1 - x^2) T_n''(x) - x T_n'(x) + n^2 T_n(x) = 0.
\]
Let \(w(x) := (x^2-1) T_n'(x)\). Show that \[
w'(x) = x T_n'(x) + n^2 T_n(x).
\]
Compute \(w'(x_j)\) for \(j = 0,\dots,n\) and conclude.
Explain why we may replace \(\lambda_j\) by \((-1)^j\) (halved for \(j = 0, n\)) in the barycentric formula. Why is this a good idea when \(n\) is large?


For 5, treat the interior nodes and the endpoints separately: \(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\) are the points where \(T_n\) attains \(\pm 1\) in \((-1,1)\). For the endpoints, evaluate the differential equation from 3 at \(x = \pm 1\) to find \(T_n'(\pm1)\).



Differentiating \(\ell_X(x) = (x - x_j) \prod_{k\not=j} (x - x_k)\) with the product rule and setting \(x = x_j\) gives \(\ell_X'(x_j) = \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j - x_k) = 1/\lambda_j\).
Differentiating \(T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos n\theta\) gives \(-\sin\theta \, T_n'(\cos\theta) = -n \sin n\theta\). Therefore, with \(x = \cos\theta\), \[
(x^2 - 1) T_n'(x) = -\sin^2\theta \cdot n \frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin \theta} = -n \sin\theta \sin n\theta = \frac{n}{2} \big( T_{n+1}(x) - T_{n-1}(x) \big)
\] by Exercise 7.5. Since both sides are polynomials which agree on \([-1,1]\), they are equal, and so \(\ell_X(x) = 2^{-n}\big( T_{n+1}(x) - T_{n-1}(x) \big) = \frac{2^{1-n}}{n} (x^2-1) T_n'(x)\).
Differentiating \(-\sin\theta \, T_n'(\cos\theta) = -n \sin n\theta\) again gives \(\sin^2\theta \, T_n''(\cos\theta) - \cos\theta \, T_n'(\cos\theta) = -n^2 \cos n\theta = -n^2 T_n(\cos\theta)\). With \(x = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin^2\theta = 1 - x^2\), this is the Chebyshev differential equation on \([-1,1]\) and therefore everywhere (both sides are polynomials).
By the product rule, \(w' = 2x T_n' + (x^2-1) T_n''\). By 3, \((x^2-1) T_n'' = n^2 T_n - x T_n'\) and so \(w' = x T_n' + n^2 T_n\).
For \(j = 1,\dots,n-1\), \(T_n(x_j) = \cos j\pi = (-1)^j\) and, since \(x_j\) is an interior maximum or minimum of \(T_n\), \(T_n'(x_j) = 0\). Therefore \(w'(x_j) = n^2 (-1)^j\).

At \(x = 1\), the differential equation gives \(-T_n'(1) + n^2 T_n(1) = 0\) and so \(T_n'(1) = n^2\). Therefore, \(w'(x_0) = w'(1) = n^2 + n^2 = 2n^2\). Similarly, at \(x = -1\), we have \(T_n'(-1) = -n^2 T_n(-1) = (-1)^{n+1} n^2\) and so \(w'(x_n) = w'(-1) = (-1)^n n^2 + (-1)^n n^2 = 2 (-1)^n n^2\).
By 1 and 2, \(\lambda_j = 1 / \ell_X'(x_j) = \frac{n 2^{n-1}}{w'(x_j)}\), which gives \[
\begin{align}
    \lambda_0 = \frac{n 2^{n-1}}{2n^2} = \frac{2^n}{4n}, \qquad
    \lambda_j = \frac{n 2^{n-1}}{(-1)^j n^2} = (-1)^j \frac{2^n}{2n}, \qquad
    \lambda_n = \frac{n 2^{n-1}}{2(-1)^n n^2} = (-1)^n \frac{2^n}{4n}. \nonumber
\end{align}
\]

The barycentric formula is unchanged if every \(\lambda_j\) is multiplied by the same constant \(c \not= 0\) (the factor \(c\) cancels between the numerator and the denominator). Taking \(c = \frac{2n}{2^n}\) gives the weights \((-1)^j\), halved for \(j = 0, n\). For large \(n\), \(2^n\) overflows in floating point arithmetic (for example, 2.0^1024 == Inf) whereas the rescaled weights are all of size \(1\) or \(\frac12\).



◆

This exercise is more difficult




Exercise 8.7 
Let \(X = \{x_0 < \dots < x_n\}\) be the equispaced nodes on \([-1,1]\): \(x_j = -1 + jh\) for \(j = 0, \dots, n\), where \(h = \frac2n\).

Show that \(\prod_{k\not= j} (x_j - x_k) = (-1)^{n-j} h^n \, j!\, (n-j)!\), and deduce that the barycentric weights are \[
\lambda_j = \frac{(-1)^{n-j}}{h^n\, n!} \binom{n}{j}.
\]
Using Exercise 8.3, explain why we may use the weights \(w_j := (-1)^j \binom{n}{j}\) in the Barycentric formula (8.3) instead. Compare the ratio \(\max_j |w_j| / \min_j |w_j|\) for these weights with the same ratio for the weights \((-1)^j \tau_j\) for Chebyshev nodes (\(\tau_j = \frac12\) for \(j = 0,n\) and \(\tau_j = 1\) otherwise) as \(n \to \infty\).
Write a function EquispacedInterpolant(f, n), analogous to ChebyshevInterpolant from the notes, which returns the polynomial interpolant of f on the equispaced nodes (using the weights \(w_j\) from 2; in Julia, binomial(n, j) computes \(\binom{n}{j}\)). Compute the maximum error \(\max_{t} |f(t) - I_Xf(t)|\) over the grid range(-1, 1, length=2001) for:

the Runge function \(f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + 25x^2}\) with \(n = 10, 20, 40\),
\(f(x) = e^x\) with \(n = 10, 20, 40, 60\).

Compare your results with the error estimate from Theorem 6.2 together with the bound \(\| \ell_X \|_{L^\infty([-1,1])} \leq \frac{e}{2\sqrt n} \big( \frac2e \big)^n\) for equispaced nodes from Lecture 6. Comment on what you see.


For 1, split the product into the terms with \(k < j\) (where \(x_j - x_k = (j - k)h > 0\)) and the terms with \(k > j\) (where \(x_j - x_k = -(k - j)h < 0\)). For 3, think about how errors of size \(10^{-16}\) in the values \(f(x_j)\) (or in the arithmetic) are amplified when the weights vary by many orders of magnitude.



For \(k < j\), we have \(x_j - x_k = (j-k)h\) and so \(\prod_{k=0}^{j-1} (x_j - x_k) = h^j \, j!\). For \(k > j\), we have \(x_j - x_k = -(k-j)h\) and so \(\prod_{k=j+1}^{n} (x_j - x_k) = (-1)^{n-j} h^{n-j} (n-j)!\). Multiplying gives \(\prod_{k\not= j} (x_j - x_k) = (-1)^{n-j} h^n \, j! \, (n-j)!\) and therefore \[
\lambda_j = \frac{(-1)^{n-j}}{h^n \, j! \, (n-j)!} = \frac{(-1)^{n-j}}{h^n \, n!} \binom{n}{j}.
\]
We have \(w_j = C \lambda_j\) with the constant \(C = (-1)^n h^n n!\) (which does not depend on \(j\)), and so the factor \(C\) cancels between the numerator and the denominator of (8.3). The smallest weights are \(|w_0| = |w_n| = 1\) and the largest is \(\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \approx 2^n \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}\). Therefore, the ratio grows exponentially: it is \(252\) for \(n = 10\), about \(1.8 \times 10^5\) for \(n = 20\), and about \(1.2 \times 10^{17}\) for \(n = 60\). For Chebyshev nodes, the ratio is \(2\) for all \(n\).
For example:

function EquispacedInterpolant( f, n )
    x = range(-1, 1, length=n+1)
    y = f.(x)
    w = [ (-1.0)^j * binomial(n, j) for j in 0:n ]

    return function ( t )
        num = 0.0
        den = 0.0
        for j ∈ 1:(n+1)
            if t == x[j]
                return y[j]
            end
            num += w[j] * y[j] / (t - x[j])
            den += w[j] / (t - x[j])
        end
        return num / den
    end
end

\(2.0 \times 10^{-1}\)
\(9.5 \times 10^{-93}\)



Here, the error bound is \(\frac{e}{(n+1)!} \cdot \frac{e}{2\sqrt n} \big(\frac2e\big)^n\) (using \(\max_{[-1,1]} |f^{(n+1)}| = e\)). For the Runge function, the error grows exponentially: this is the Runge phenomenon from Lecture 6 (the derivatives of the Runge function grow too quickly for the error estimate to give convergence). For \(e^x\), the exact interpolant converges extremely quickly, and the computed error decreases until \(n \approx 20\). After that, the computed error grows even though the exact interpolant is more and more accurate. This is caused by rounding errors: perturbing the data \(f(x_j)\) by \(\delta_j\) changes the interpolant by \(\sum_j \delta_j \ell_j(x)\), and for equispaced nodes \(\max_x \sum_j |\ell_j(x)|\) grows exponentially in \(n\) (like the ratio of the weights in 2). Rounding errors of size \(10^{-16}\) are therefore amplified by a factor of order \(2^n\). For Chebyshev nodes, this amplification factor only grows like \(\log n\) (see Berrut and Trefethen (2004)).






Berrut, Jean-Paul, and Lloyd N. Trefethen. 2004. “Barycentric Lagrange Interpolation.” SIAM Review 46 (3): 501–17. https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036144502417715.


Higham, Nicholas J. 2004. “The Numerical Stability of Barycentric Lagrange Interpolation.” IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 24 (4): 547–56. https://doi.org/10.1093/imanum/24.4.547.

title: 9  Hermite interpolation
text:
Barycentric formula: for \(x \not\in X\), \(I_Xf(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j f(x_j)}{x - x_j} \Big/ \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\lambda_j}{x - x_j}\) where \(\lambda_j = \prod_{k\not=j} (x_j - x_k)^{-1}\),
Barycentric formula requires \(O(n)\) operations per evaluation and is numerically stable for Chebyshev nodes (with weights \((-1)^j\), halved for \(j = 0, n\)),
Divided differences: \(f[x_0,\dots,x_n]\) is the leading coefficient of \(I_Xf\); it doesn’t depend on the ordering of the nodes and is linear in \(f\),
Recursion: \(f[x_0,\dots,x_n] = \frac{f[x_1,\dots,x_n] - f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]}{x_n - x_0}\) (Theorem 8.2),
Newton form: \(I_Xf = \sum_{k=0}^n f[x_0,\dots,x_k] \, \pi_k\) where \(\pi_k(x) = (x-x_0)\cdots(x-x_{k-1})\) (Theorem 8.3),
The coefficients can be read off from the divided difference table; adding a new node only adds one new term.


Exercise. Exercise 8.6

title: 9  Hermite interpolation
text:
9.2 Hermite Interpolation
Now consider distinct nodes \(z_0, \dots, z_k\) with multiplicities \(m_0, \dots, m_k \geq 1\) and let \(X = \{\{ x_0, \dots, x_n \}\}\) be the multiset in which each \(z_j\) appears \(m_j\) times (so that \(n+1 = \sum_{j=0}^k m_j\)).
Hermite: find \(p\) such that, for \(j = 0, \dots, k\),
\[
\begin{align}
    p(z_j) &= f(z_j),  \nonumber\\
    p'(z_j) &= f'(z_j),  \nonumber\\
    &\vdots \nonumber\\
    p^{(m_j-1)}(z_j) &= f^{(m_j-1)}(z_j).
\end{align}
\]
When \(m_j = 1\) for all \(j\), this is the Lagrange interpolation problem.

Exercise 9.1 
Let \(f(x) = e^x\) and \(X = \{\{0, 0, 1\}\}\) (so that \(z_0 = 0\) with \(m_0 = 2\), \(z_1 = 1\) with \(m_1 = 1\), and \(n = 2\)). Find the Hermite interpolant \(p \in \mathcal P_2\) of \(f\) on \(X\) by writing \(p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2\) and solving for the coefficients. Compare \(p\) with the Taylor polynomial of degree \(1\) about \(0\) and with the Lagrange interpolant of \(f\) on \(\{0, 1\}\).


Exercise 9.2 
What is the least degree polynomial interpolant on \(X = \{\{x_0, x_0, \dots, x_0\}\}\) (where \(x_0\) is repeated \(n+1\) times)?


Theorem 9.1 There exists a unique polynomial of degree at most \(n\) solving the Hermite interpolation problem.


Proof. See Exercise 9.5.

Again, we define the divided differences (but now for the more general case where we may have repeated interpolation nodes):

Definition 9.1 We define the divided difference \(f[x_{0}, \dots, x_n]\) to be the leading coefficient in the polynomial interpolation \(p\in \mathcal P_n\) solving the Hermite interpolation problem for \(f\) on \(X\):
\[
\begin{align}
    p(x) = f[x_0,\dots,x_n] x^n + q(x)
\end{align}
\]
where \(q \in \mathcal P_{n-1}\) and \(p^{(l)}(z_j) = f^{(l)}(z_j)\) for \(l = 0,\dots,m_j-1\) and \(j = 0, \dots, k\).


Theorem 9.2 Suppose that \(f\) is sufficiently differentiable (\(f \in C^{m-1}\) where \(m := \max_j m_j\)). Then, we have
\[
\begin{align}
    f[x_0, \dots, x_n] &= \begin{cases}
    \frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!} & \text{if } x_0 = x_1 = \dots = x_n \\
    \frac
        {f[x_1, \dots, x_n] - f[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}]}
        {x_n - x_0} &\text{if } x_0 \not= x_n
    \end{cases}
\end{align}
\]
If the nodes are not all equal, we can always reorder \(X\) so that \(x_0 \not= x_n\) (the divided difference does not depend on the ordering of the nodes).

Proof

Proof. You have seen above that the Taylor polynomial
\[
\begin{align}
    T_f(x) =\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{f^{(j)}(x_0)}{j!}(x - x_0)^j
\end{align}
\]
solves the Hermite interpolation problem on \(X = \{\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}\}\) in the case where \(x_0 = \dots = x_n\). For such \(X\), the leading coefficient in this expression is \(f[x_{0}, \dots, x_n] = \frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!}\).
For the second case, suppose \(x_0 \not= x_n\). We adapt the proof of Theorem 8.2.
Ordering and linearity. The Hermite interpolation problem (and so, by Theorem 9.1, its unique solution) only depends on the multiset \(X\) and not on how we label its elements. Therefore \(f[x_0,\dots,x_n]\) does not depend on the ordering of the nodes. Moreover, if \(p\) and \(q\) are the Hermite interpolants of \(f\) and \(g\) on \(X\), then \(p + cq \in \mathcal P_n\) satisfies the Hermite conditions for \(f + cg\), and so \((f + cg)[x_0,\dots,x_n] = f[x_0,\dots,x_n] + c\, g[x_0,\dots,x_n]\).
Multiplying by \((x - x_n)\). Let \(p \in \mathcal P_{n-1}\) be the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(X' := \{\{x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}\}\}\) and define \(g(x) := (x - x_n) f(x)\) and \(q(x) := (x - x_n) p(x) \in \mathcal P_n\). We claim that \(q\) is the Hermite interpolant of \(g\) on \(X\). Let \(u := p - f\). By the product rule, \[
    q^{(l)}(x) - g^{(l)}(x) = \frac{\mathrm d^l}{\mathrm dx^l} \big[ (x - x_n) u(x) \big] = (x - x_n) u^{(l)}(x) + l \, u^{(l-1)}(x)
\] (where the second term is absent when \(l = 0\)). Let \(z\) be a node which appears \(m\) times in \(X'\), so that \(u^{(i)}(z) = 0\) for \(i = 0, \dots, m-1\).

If \(z \not= x_n\), then \(z\) also appears \(m\) times in \(X\). For \(l \leq m - 1\), we have \(u^{(l)}(z) = u^{(l-1)}(z) = 0\), and so \(q^{(l)}(z) = g^{(l)}(z)\).
If \(z = x_n\), then \(z\) appears \(m + 1\) times in \(X\) (with \(m = 0\) if \(x_n \not\in X'\)). For \(l \leq m\), the first term vanishes because \(z - x_n = 0\), and the second term vanishes because \(l - 1 \leq m - 1\) (or \(l = 0\)). Therefore \(q^{(l)}(x_n) = g^{(l)}(x_n)\) for \(l = 0, \dots, m\).

So \(q\) satisfies all of the Hermite conditions for \(g\) on \(X\) and, by Theorem 9.1, it is the Hermite interpolant of \(g\) on \(X\). Comparing leading coefficients, the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(q\) is both \(g[x_0, \dots, x_n]\) and the coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\) in \(p\), that is, \(f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]\). Therefore \[
    \big( (x - x_n) f \big)[x_0, \dots, x_n] = f[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}].
\] Applying this to the reordered multiset \(\{\{x_1, \dots, x_n, x_0\}\}\) gives \(\big( (x - x_0) f \big)[x_0, \dots, x_n] = f[x_1, \dots, x_n]\).
Conclusion. Since \((x - x_0) f(x) - (x - x_n) f(x) = (x_n - x_0) f(x)\), linearity gives \[
    (x_n - x_0) f[x_0,\dots,x_n] = \big( (x - x_0) f \big)[x_0, \dots, x_n] - \big( (x - x_n) f \big)[x_0, \dots, x_n] = f[x_1, \dots, x_n] - f[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}].
\] Dividing by \(x_n - x_0 \not= 0\) gives the result.


For distinct nodes, this is exactly the proof of Theorem 8.2 (where only the case \(l = 0\) appears).

title: 9  Hermite interpolation
section: 9.3 Newton form and divided difference table with repeated nodes
text:
9.3 Newton form and divided difference table with repeated nodes
The Newton form from Theorem 8.3 still holds when nodes are repeated. As before, let \(\pi_0(x) = 1\) and \(\pi_k(x) = (x - x_0)(x-x_1)\cdots(x - x_{k-1})\), where repeated nodes now give repeated factors (e.g. for \(X = \{\{0,0,\pi,\pi\}\}\) we have \(\pi_2(x) = x^2\) and \(\pi_3(x) = x^2 (x - \pi)\)).

Theorem 9.3 Let \(X = \{\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}\}\) be a multiset and \(f\) sufficiently differentiable. Then the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(X\) is \[
    p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n f[x_0,\dots,x_k] \, \pi_k(x).
\]


Proof. The same as for Theorem 8.3: let \(p_k \in \mathcal P_k\) be the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(\{\{x_0,\dots,x_k\}\}\). Then \(p_k - p_{k-1} \in \mathcal P_k\) satisfies the Hermite conditions with zero data on \(\{\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}\}\), and so it has a zero of order \(m\) at every node appearing \(m\) times in \(\{\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}\}\) (see Exercise 9.5, part 1). Therefore \(p_k - p_{k-1} = c_k \pi_k\) and comparing the coefficients of \(x^k\) gives \(c_k = f[x_0,\dots,x_k]\).

To compute the divided difference table, list the nodes so that equal nodes are next to each other. Then every entry \(f[x_j,\dots,x_{j+k}]\) is computed using Theorem 9.2: if \(x_j = x_{j+k}\) (so that all of the nodes involved are equal), it is \(\frac{f^{(k)}(x_j)}{k!}\); otherwise it is the usual difference quotient of its two neighbours in the previous column. In particular, the first column contains \(f[x_j, x_{j+1}] = f'(x_j)\) whenever \(x_j = x_{j+1}\).

Exercise 9.3 
Return to Exercise 9.1: compute the Hermite interpolant of \(f(x) = e^x\) on \(\{\{0, 0, 1\}\}\) again, this time using the divided difference table and Theorem 9.3.


Exercise 9.4 
What is the Hermite interpolant of \(f(x) = \sin x\) on \(\{\{ 0,0,\pi, \pi\}\}\)? Hint: you can compute the divided difference tables in the same way as before.

9.4 Extra exercises

Exercise 9.5 
In this exercise, we prove Theorem 9.1. As in the notes, let \(z_0, \dots, z_k\) be distinct nodes with multiplicities \(m_0, \dots, m_k \geq 1\), and let \(n + 1 = \sum_{j=0}^k m_j\).

Let \(r \in \mathcal P_n\) and suppose that \(r^{(l)}(z) = 0\) for \(l = 0, \dots, m-1\). Show that \(r(x) = (x - z)^m s(x)\) for some polynomial \(s\).
Suppose that \(r \in \mathcal P_n\) satisfies \(r^{(l)}(z_j) = 0\) for all \(l = 0,\dots,m_j - 1\) and \(j = 0,\dots,k\). Show that \(r = 0\).
Deduce that the Hermite interpolation problem has at most one solution in \(\mathcal P_n\).
Consider the map \(L : \mathcal P_n \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) defined by \(L p := \big( p^{(l)}(z_j) \big)_{j = 0,\dots,k, \; l = 0, \dots, m_j - 1}\). Show that \(L\) is linear and injective, and conclude that the Hermite interpolation problem has exactly one solution in \(\mathcal P_n\).


For 1, write \(r\) as its Taylor polynomial about \(z\) (which is exact because \(r\) is a polynomial). For 2, apply 1 at \(z_0\) and then show that \(s\) still has zeros of order \(m_j\) at \(z_j\) for \(j \geq 1\). For 4, recall that an injective linear map between vector spaces of the same finite dimension is also surjective.



Since \(r \in \mathcal P_n\), Taylor’s theorem is exact: \(r(x) = \sum_{l=0}^n \frac{r^{(l)}(z)}{l!} (x - z)^l = \sum_{l=m}^n \frac{r^{(l)}(z)}{l!} (x - z)^l = (x-z)^m s(x)\) where \(s(x) := \sum_{l=m}^n \frac{r^{(l)}(z)}{l!} (x - z)^{l-m}\).
By 1, \(r(x) = (x - z_0)^{m_0} s_0(x)\). Fix \(j \geq 1\) and write \(u(x) := (x - z_0)^{m_0}\) (so that \(u(z_j) \not= 0\) because the nodes are distinct). By the Leibniz rule, \[
r^{(l)}(z_j) = \sum_{i=0}^l \binom{l}{i} u^{(l-i)}(z_j) \, s_0^{(i)}(z_j) = u(z_j) \, s_0^{(l)}(z_j) + \sum_{i=0}^{l-1} \binom{l}{i} u^{(l-i)}(z_j) \, s_0^{(i)}(z_j).
\] By induction on \(l = 0, \dots, m_j - 1\), we obtain \(s_0^{(l)}(z_j) = 0\). Therefore, \(s_0\) satisfies the same conditions at \(z_1, \dots, z_k\) and, repeating the argument, we have \[
r(x) = (x - z_0)^{m_0} (x - z_1)^{m_1} \cdots (x - z_k)^{m_k} s(x)
\] for some polynomial \(s\). If \(s \not= 0\), then \(r\) has degree at least \(\sum_j m_j = n+1\), which contradicts \(r \in \mathcal P_n\). Therefore \(s = 0\) and \(r = 0\).
If \(p, q \in \mathcal P_n\) both solve the Hermite interpolation problem, then \(r := p - q \in \mathcal P_n\) satisfies \(r^{(l)}(z_j) = f^{(l)}(z_j) - f^{(l)}(z_j) = 0\) for all \(j\) and \(l = 0, \dots, m_j-1\). By 2, \(r = 0\) and so \(p = q\).
Differentiation and evaluation are linear and so \(L\) is linear. If \(L p = 0\), then \(p = 0\) by 2, and so \(L\) is injective. Since \(\dim \mathcal P_n = n + 1 = \dim \mathbb R^{n+1}\), the rank-nullity theorem shows that \(L\) is also surjective. In particular, there exists \(p \in \mathcal P_n\) with \(L p = \big( f^{(l)}(z_j) \big)_{j,l}\), which is exactly a solution to the Hermite interpolation problem. By 3, this solution is unique.




Exercise 9.6 
In this exercise, we prove the error estimate for Hermite interpolation (compare with the Lagrange case in Lecture 6). We say that \(g\) has a zero of order \(m\) at \(z\) if \(g(z) = g'(z) = \dots = g^{(m-1)}(z) = 0\).

(Rolle’s theorem with multiplicities) Suppose that \(g \in C^1([a,b])\) has zeros at distinct points \(w_1 < \dots < w_r\) in \([a,b]\) of orders \(k_1, \dots, k_r\), and let \(N := k_1 + \dots + k_r\). Show that \(g'\) has zeros in \([w_1, w_r]\) whose orders add up to at least \(N - 1\).
Let \(f \in C^{n+1}([a,b])\), let \(X = \{\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}\} \subset [a,b]\) be a multiset, and let \(p \in \mathcal P_n\) be the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(X\). Define the node polynomial \(\ell_X(x) := (x - x_0)(x - x_1) \cdots (x - x_n)\) (so repeated nodes give repeated factors). Show that, for every \(x \in [a,b]\), there exists \(\xi_x \in [\min (\{x\} \cup X), \max (\{x\} \cup X)]\) with \[
f(x) - p(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!} \ell_X(x).
\]

This exercise is more difficult




Exercise 9.7 (Cubic Hermite interpolation) 
Let \(X = \{\{0, 0, 1, 1\}\}\) and suppose that we know \(f(0) = y_0\), \(f'(0) = s_0\), \(f(1) = y_1\) and \(f'(1) = s_1\).

Compute the divided difference table and show that the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(X\) is \[
p(x) = y_0 + s_0 x + (d - s_0) x^2 + (s_0 + s_1 - 2d) \, x^2 (x - 1), \qquad \text{where } d := y_1 - y_0.
\]
Write down \(p\) for \(f(x) = e^x\) and compare it with Exercise 9.1.
Use Exercise 9.6 to show that \(\max_{x \in [0,1]} |e^x - p(x)| \leq \frac{e}{384}\).
More generally, suppose that \(p\) is the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(\{\{a, a, b, b\}\}\). Show that \(\max_{x \in [a,b]} |f(x) - p(x)| \leq \frac{(b-a)^4}{384} \max_{[a,b]} |f^{(4)}|\). What does this tell you about approximating \(f\) on \([a,b]\) by a cubic Hermite interpolant on each of \(N\) subintervals of length \(h = \frac{b-a}{N}\)?



Exercise 9.8 

Let \(f \in C^n([a,b])\) and let \(X = \{\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}\} \subset [a,b]\) be a multiset. Show that there exists \(\xi \in [\min X, \max X]\) with \[
f[x_0, \dots, x_n] = \frac{f^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}.
\]
Deduce that \(f[x_0, x_0 + h] \to f'(x_0)\) and, more generally, \(f[x_0, x_0 + h, \dots, x_0 + nh] \to \frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!}\) as \(h \to 0\). Explain why this makes the first case of Theorem 9.2 a natural definition.

Exercise 9.9 

Write a Julia function hermite_dd(x, df) which takes a vector of nodes x (sorted so that equal nodes are next to each other) and a function df(l, z) returning \(f^{(l)}(z)\), and returns the Newton coefficients \(f[x_0], f[x_0,x_1], \dots, f[x_0,\dots,x_n]\) using the divided difference table.
Write a function newton_eval(c, x, t) which evaluates \(\sum_{k=0}^n c_k \pi_k(t)\) using \(O(n)\) operations.
Check your code against Exercise 9.1, Exercise 9.4, and Exercise 9.7, and compute \(\max_{t \in [0,1]} |e^t - p(t)|\) for the cubic Hermite interpolant of \(e^x\) on \(\{\{0,0,1,1\}\}\).

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
Hermite interpolation: given distinct nodes \(z_0,\dots,z_k\) with multiplicities \(m_0,\dots,m_k\) (forming a multiset \(X = \{\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}\}\)), find \(p \in \mathcal P_n\) with \(p^{(l)}(z_j) = f^{(l)}(z_j)\) for \(l = 0,\dots,m_j-1\),
There exists a unique solution (Theorem 9.1); Taylor expansion (one node repeated \(n+1\) times) and Lagrange interpolation (all \(m_j = 1\)) are the two extremes,
Divided differences with repeated nodes: \(f[x_0,\dots,x_n] = \frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!}\) if all nodes are equal, otherwise the usual recursion (Theorem 9.2),
Newton form \(p = \sum_{k=0}^n f[x_0,\dots,x_k] \, \pi_k\) (Theorem 9.3) computed from the divided difference table,
Error estimate: \(f(x) - p(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!} \ell_X(x)\) where \(\ell_X(x) = (x-x_0)\cdots(x-x_n)\) (Exercise 9.6).


Exercise. Exercise 9.7


Exercise 10.1 (Recap of last week) 

Compute the divided difference table for \(f(x) = x^2\) on \(\{0, 1, 2\}\) and write down the Newton form of the interpolant. What do you notice?
What are \(f[x_0, x_0]\) and \(f[x_0, x_0, x_0]\)?
Why do we prefer the barycentric formula (8.3) to the naive Lagrange formula?
What is the Hermite interpolant of \(f\) on \(\{\{a, a\}\}\)? How many conditions does the Hermite interpolant on \(\{\{0, 0, 1\}\}\) satisfy, and what is its degree?
The next iterate of Newton’s method is the root of which interpolant of \(f\)? What about the secant method?



\(f[0] = f(0) = 0\), \(f[1] = f(1) = 1\), \(f[2] = f(2) = 4\); \(f[0,1] = \frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0} = 1\), \(f[1,2] = \frac{f(1)-f(2)}{1-2} = 3\); \(f[0,1,2] = \frac{f[1,2] - f[0,1]}{2-0} = \frac{3 - 1}{2 - 0} = 1\). So \(p(x) = 0 + 1 \cdot x + 1 \cdot x(x-1) = x^2\): the interpolant is \(f\) itself, as it must be since \(f \in \mathcal P_2\).
\(f[x_0, x_0] = f'(x_0)\) and \(f[x_0, x_0, x_0] = \frac{f''(x_0)}{2}\).
Once the weights are known, the barycentric formula costs \(O(n)\) operations per evaluation (the naive formula costs \(O(n^2)\)), it is numerically stable, and the weights may be rescaled to avoid overflow/underflow (Exercise 8.1, Exercise 8.3).
The tangent line \(p(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\) (the degree \(1\) Taylor polynomial). On \(\{\{0,0,1\}\}\) there are \(3\) conditions (\(p(0) = f(0)\), \(p'(0) = f'(0)\), \(p(1) = f(1)\)) and \(p \in \mathcal P_2\).
Newton: \(x_{n+1}\) is the root of the Hermite interpolant on \(\{\{x_n, x_n\}\}\) (the tangent line). Secant: \(x_{n+1}\) is the root of the Lagrange interpolant on \(\{x_{n-1}, x_n\}\) (the secant line).

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
10.2 Quadrature rules

Exercise 10.2 (Why approximate integrals?) 
Can you compute \(\int_0^1 e^{-x^2} \,\mathrm{d}x\) or \(\int_0^1 \frac{\sin x}{x} \,\mathrm{d}x\) exactly?

No: neither integrand has an antiderivative that can be written in terms of elementary functions. (Also, in practice we may only know \(f\) at some points.) This is why we need quadrature rules.
(One defines
\[\begin{align}
    \mathrm{erf}(x) &:= \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^x e^{-t^2} \mathrm{d}t \nonumber\\
    %
    \mathrm{Si}(x) &:= \int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{t} \mathrm{d}t
\end{align}\]
with \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\mathrm{erf}(x)=1\) and \(\mathrm{Si}(x) \to \frac{\pi}{2}\).)



Definition 10.1 We wish to consider quadrature rules of the following form:
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_{a}^b f &\approx \sum_j w_j f(x_j).
\end{align}
\tag{10.1}\]
We call \(\{w_j\}\) the quadrature weights, \(\{x_j\}\) the quadrature nodes and \((\{w_j\}, \{x_j\})\) or \(\sum_{j} w_j f(x_j)\) a quadrature rule.

Suppose \(p = I_X f\) is the polynomial of degree at most \(n\) interpolating \(f\) on \(X = \{x_0,\dots,x_n \}\): that is \(p(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n \ell_j(x) f(x_j)\). We simply approximate the integral of \(f\) by instead integrating \(p\):
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_{a}^b f &\approx \int_a^b p \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \sum_{j=0}^n \Big[\int_a^b\ell_j(x)\mathrm{d}x \Big] f(x_j)
\end{align}
\tag{10.2}\]
which gives a quadrature rule with weights \(w_j := \int_a^b\ell_j(x)\mathrm{d}x\) and nodes \(x_j\).

Definition 10.2 When the interpolation nodes \(x_0, \dots, x_n\) are equispaced, (10.2) is a Newton–Cotes quadrature rule.


Example 10.1 In the following, we will consider the example of integrating \(f(x) = \tfrac1{2\pi} ( x + x \sin x)\) between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). In this particular case, the integral is \(\pi-1\). We use this example so that we can analyse the error committed in the methods we will introduce.


Exercise 10.3 
Show that \(\int_0^{2\pi} \frac{1}{2\pi}(x + x \sin x) \,\mathrm{d}x = \pi - 1\).

Integrating by parts gives
\[\begin{align}
\int_0^{2\pi} x \sin x \,\mathrm{d}x
%
&= \int_0^{2\pi} x (-\cos' x) \,\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
%
&= \big[ -x \cos x \big]_0^{2\pi} + \int_0^{2\pi} \cos x \,\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
%
&= -2\pi.
\end{align}\]
Therefore the integral of \((x+x\sin x)/2\pi\) on \([0,2\pi]\) is \(\frac{1}{2\pi} \big( 2\pi^2 - 2\pi \big) = \pi - 1\).




Code
a, b = 0, 2π
f = x -> x * ( 1 + sin(x) ) /( 2π )
df_max = 1 + 1/(2π)

# maximum of |f''|, |f'''|, |f''''| on [a,b] (computed on a fine grid)
d2f = x -> ( 2cos(x) - x * sin(x) ) /( 2π )
d3f = x -> ( -3sin(x) - x * cos(x) ) /( 2π )
d4f = x -> ( -4cos(x) + x * sin(x) ) /( 2π )
X = range(a, b, 10^5)
d2f_max = maximum( abs.( d2f.(X) ) )
d3f_max = maximum( abs.( d3f.(X) ) )
d4f_max = maximum( abs.( d4f.(X) ) )
plot( f, a, b, title=L"f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} (x + x\sin x ) ", lw = 3, legend=false)

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
10.3 Rectangular rule
The simplest rule of this kind is taking \(X = \{a\}\) and considering the polynomial interpolation of degree \(0\): \(p_0(x) = f(a)\),
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_a^b f(x)\mathrm{d}x &\approx \int_a^b p_0(x)\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
    &= (b-a) f(a).
\end{align}
\tag{10.3}\]
The rule has weights \(\{ b-a \}\) and nodes \(\{ a \}\). Notice that this rule is exact if \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(0\).

Exercise 10.4 (Interpolation error with one node) 
Write down the interpolation error formula for \(f - p\) when \(p\) interpolates \(f\) on \(n+1\) nodes (Theorem 6.2). What does it say when \(n = 0\) and \(X = \{a\}\)?

We have: for \(x\), there exists \(\xi_x\) between \(\min\{ x, \min X\}\) and \(\max\{x,\max X\}\) such that
\[\begin{align}
f(x) - p(x) &= \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!} \ell_X(x)
\end{align}\]
where \(\ell_X\) is the node polynomial on \(X\). For \(n = 0\) and \(X = \{a\}\), \(p = f(a)\) and this reads \(f(x) - f(a) = f'(\xi_x)(x - a)\) for some \(\xi_x\) between \(a\) and \(x\) (which is just the mean value theorem)



Exercise 10.5 (Error estimate) 
Suppose \(f \in C^1([a,b])\). Show that
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_{a}^b f - (b-a) f(a) \right| \leq \| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \frac{(b-a)^2}{2}.
\end{align}
\]

Since \(p_0\) is a degree zero interpolating polynomial, we may apply the error bound we had for interpolation (Theorem 6.2):
\[
\begin{align}
    f(x) - p_0(x) = f'(\xi_x) (x - a)
\end{align}
\]
for some \(\xi_x \in [a, x]\) (in this case, this is just the mean value theorem). Therefore, integrating this over \([a,b]\), we have the bound
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_{a}^b \big[ f(x) - p_0(x) \big] \mathrm{d}x \right|
    %
    &\leq \| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \int_a^b |x - a| \mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
    &= \| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \int_{0}^{b-a} t \,\mathrm{d}t \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \frac{(b-a)^2}{2}. \nonumber
\end{align}
\]


Composite rule. This error bound is only useful if \([a,b]\) is a small interval (or \(f'\) is small). It therefore makes sense to split the interval \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals and consider the rectangular rule on each one: consider \(x_j = a + j\frac{b-a}{n}\) for \(j = 0,\dots,n\) and write
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_a^b f &= \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \int_{x_j}^{x_{j+1}} f \nonumber\\
    %
    &\approx \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (x_{j+1} - x_j) f(x_j).
\end{align}
\]
This is a quadrature rule with weights \(w_j = x_{j+1} - x_j = \frac{b-a}{n}\) and nodes \(x_j\) for \(j = 0,\dots,n-1\).

Exercise 10.6 
Approximate \(\int_0^1 x \,\mathrm{d}x\) by the composite rectangular rule with \(n\) subintervals of equal length. What is the error?

First, note that \(\int_0^1 x \mathrm{d}x = \frac12\).
The composite rectangular rule on \([0,1]\) is \(\frac1n \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{j}{n} = \frac{n-1}{2n} = \frac12 - \frac{1}{2n}\), so the error is exactly \(\frac{1}{2n}\): the rate \(O(n^{-1})\) of Theorem 10.1 (and the constant \(\frac{\|f'\|_{L^\infty}}{2}(b-a)^2 = \frac12\) is attained).



Theorem 10.1 Suppose \(f \in C^1([a,b])\). Then the composite rectangular rule satisfies
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_a^b f - \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{b-a}{n} f(x_j) \right| &\leq   \frac{\| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \frac{ (b-a)^2 }{ n }.
\end{align}
\]


Proof. Using Exercise 10.5 on each subinterval \([x_j, x_{j+1}]\) and summing over \(j\), we obtain
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_a^b f - \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{b-a}{n} f(x_j) \right| &\leq  \| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac12 \Big(\frac{b-a}{n}\Big)^2 \nonumber\\
    %
    &=   \frac{\| f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \frac{ (b-a)^2 }{ n }. \nonumber
\end{align}
\]


Remark 10.1. Notice that this quadrature rule is exact if \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(0\).

Numerics. We now test this numerically:


Code
N = 50
R = []

anim = @animate for n ∈ 1:N
    
    h = (b-a)/n
    x = [a + j*(b-a)/n for j in 0:n]
    
    push!( R, sum( [ ( x[j+1] - x[j] ) * f( x[j] ) for j in 1:n] ) )
    
    plot( f, a, b, label=L"x( 1 + \sin(x) )/2π", lw = 3)

    for m ∈ 1:n 
        plot!([x[m], x[m+1]], [f(x[m]), f(x[m])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
        plot!([x[m], x[m]], [0, f(x[m])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
        plot!([x[m+1], x[m+1]], [0, f(x[m])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
    end

end

gif(anim, "../images/Rectangular.gif", fps = 1, show_msg = false)







Code
scatter( abs.(R .- (π -1)), xaxis=:log, yaxis=:log, markersize=5, label="error", title="Error estimate" )
plot!( (1/2)*df_max*(b-a)^2*(1:N).^(-1), linestyle=:dash,label="error bound" )

plot!( 4*(1:N).^(-1), linestyle=:dash, label=L"4n^{-1}" )





We can see here that the error decays with rate \(O(n^{-1})\) and the error bound (proved above) is in fact an upper bound!

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
10.4 Trapezoid rule
The next simplest rule of this kind is taking \(X = \{a, b\}\) and considering the polynomial interpolation \(p_1\) of degree \(1\):
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_a^b f(x) \mathrm{d}x
    %
    &\approx \int_a^b p_1(x) \mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
    %
    &= \frac{b-a}{2} \big( f(a) + f(b) \big).
\end{align}
\]
When \(f(a), f(b) \geq 0\), this is the area of the trapezium with vertices \((a,0), (a,f(a)), (b, f(b)), (b,0)\): width \(b-a\) times the average height \(\frac{f(a) + f(b)}{2}\).
This rule has weights \(\{ \frac{b-a}{2}, \frac{b-a}{2} \}\) and nodes \(\{ a, b \}\). Notice that this rule is exact if \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(1\) (because \(f\) agrees with \(p_1\) in this case).

Exercise 10.7 

Write down the polynomial \(p_1\) of degree at most \(1\) interpolating \(f\) on \(X = \{a, b\}\).
Show that \(\int_a^b p_1(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{b-a}{2} \big( f(a) + f(b) \big)\).


You can either go through the details in the integration, or draw a picture and calculate the area of the trapezium with points \((a,0), (a,f(a)), (b, f(b)), (b,0)\). If you do the integration explicitly, the Newton form is probably slightly easier…


Lagrange form:

We have \(p_1(x) = \frac{x-b}{a-b}f(a) + \frac{x-a}{b-a} f(b)\).
We have \[
\begin{align}
\int_a^b \frac{x-b}{a-b} \,\mathrm{d}x
%
&= \frac{1}{a-b} \Big[ \frac{(x-b)^2}{2} \Big]_a^b
%
\nonumber\\
%
&= - \frac{(a-b)^2}{2(a-b)} = \frac{b-a}{2}
\nonumber\\
\int_a^b \frac{x-a}{b-a} \,\mathrm{d}x &= \frac{1}{b-a} \Big[ \frac{(x-a)^2}{2} \Big]_a^b
\nonumber\\
&= \frac{b-a}{2}, \nonumber
\end{align}
\] and so \(\int_a^b p_1 = \frac{b-a}{2} f(a) + \frac{b-a}{2} f(b)\).

Newton form:

\(p_1(x) = f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} (x-a)\),
Integrating gives \[
\begin{align}
\int_a^b (x-a) \mathrm{d}x &= \frac12 (x-a)^2\Big|_a^b \nonumber\\
%
&= \frac12 (b-a)^2
\end{align}
\] and the result follows.




Exercise 10.8 
What is the sign of \((x-a)(x-b)\) on \([a,b]\)? Compute \(\int_a^b |(x-a)(x-b)| \,\mathrm{d}x\).

Make the substitution \(t := x - \frac{a+b}{2}\) and define \(h := b-a\).


We have \((x-a)(x-b) \leq 0\) on \([a,b]\), so
\[\begin{align}
\int_a^b |(x-a)(x-b)| \,\mathrm{d}x
%
&= -\int_a^b (x-a)(x-b) \,\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
%
&= \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} \big( \tfrac{h^2}{4} -t^2 \big) \mathrm{d}t \nonumber\\
%
&= \tfrac{h^3}{4} - \Big[ \frac{t^3}{3} \Big]_{-h/2}^{h/2} \nonumber\\
%
&= \tfrac{h^3}{4} - \frac{h^3}{12}
\nonumber\\
%
&= \frac{(b-a)^3}{6}.
\end{align}\]



Theorem 10.2 (Error estimate) Suppose \(f \in C^2([a,b])\). Then
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_{a}^b f - \frac{b-a}{2} \big( f(a) + f(b) \big) \right| \leq \frac{\| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{12} (b-a)^3.
\end{align}
\]


Proof. Since \(p_1\) is a degree one interpolating polynomial, we may apply the error bound we had for interpolation (Theorem 6.2):
\[
\begin{align}
    f(x) - p_1(x) = \frac{f''(\xi_x)}{2} (x - a)(x-b)
\end{align}
\]
for some \(\xi_x \in [a, b]\). Therefore, integrating this over \([a,b]\), we have the bound
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_{a}^b \big[ f(x) - p_1(x) \big] \mathrm{d}x \right|
    %
    &\leq \frac{\| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \int_a^b |(x - a)(x-b)| \mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
    &= \frac{\| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \frac{(b-a)^3}{6} \nonumber
\end{align}
\]
(see Exercise 10.8 for the last integral).

Composite rule. This error bound is only useful if \([a,b]\) is a small interval (or \(f''\) is small). It therefore makes sense to split the interval \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals and consider the trapezium rule on each one: consider \(x_j = a + j\frac{b-a}{n}\) for \(j = 0,\dots,n\) and write
\[
\begin{align}
    \int_a^b f(x) \mathrm{d}x &= \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \int_{x_j}^{x_{j+1}} f(x)\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
    %
    &\approx \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{x_{j+1} - x_j}{2} \big[ f(x_j) + f(x_{j+1}) \big].
\end{align}
\]
This is a quadrature rule with weights \(w_0 = w_n = \frac{x_{1} - x_0}{2} = \frac{b-a}{2n}\) and \(w_j = \frac{b-a}{n}\) for \(j=1,\dots,n-1\).

Theorem 10.3 Suppose \(f \in C^2([a,b])\). Then the composite trapezoid rule satisfies
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_a^b f - \frac{b-a}{n} {\sum_{0 \leq j \leq n}}^\prime f(x_j) \right| &\leq   \frac{\| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{12} \frac{ (b-a)^3 }{ n^2 }
\end{align}
\]
where \(\sum^\prime\) indicates that the first and last terms must be multiplied by \(\frac12\).


Proof. Using Theorem 10.2 on each subinterval and summing over \(j\), we obtain
\[
\begin{align}
    \left| \int_a^b f - \frac{b-a}{n} {\sum_{0 \leq j \leq n}}^\prime f(x_j) \right| &\leq  \| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac1{12} \left(\frac{b-a}{n}\right)^3 \nonumber\\
    %
    &=   \frac{\| f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{12} \frac{ (b-a)^3 }{ n^2 }. \nonumber
\end{align}
\]


Remark 10.2. Notice that this quadrature rule is exact if \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(1\).

Numerics. We now test this numerically:


Code
N = 30
T = []

anim = @animate for n ∈ 1:N
    
    h = (b-a)/n
    x = [a + j*(b-a)/n for j in 0:n]
    
    push!( T, sum( [ (1/2)*( x[j+1] - x[j] ) * ( f(x[j]) + f(x[j+1]) ) for j in 1:n] ) )
    
    plot( f, a, b, label=L"x( 1 + \sin(x) )/2π", lw = 3)

    for m ∈ 1:n 
        plot!([x[m], x[m+1]], [f(x[m]), f(x[m+1])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
        plot!([x[m], x[m]], [0, f(x[m])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
        plot!([x[m+1], x[m+1]], [0, f(x[m+1])], lw=3, color="red", primary=false)
    end

end

gif(anim, "../images/Trapezium.gif", fps = 1, show_msg = false)







Code
scatter( abs.(T .- (π -1)), xaxis=:log, yaxis=:log, markersize=5, label="error" )
plot!( (1/12)*d2f_max*(b-a)^3*(1:N).^(-2), linestyle=:dash, label="error bound" )
plot!( 5*(1:N).^(-2), linestyle=:dash, label=L"5n^{-2}" )  





We can see here that the error decays with rate \(O(n^{-2})\) and the error bound (proved above) is in fact an upper bound!

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
10.5 Summary

Rectangular rule is given by \((b-a) f(a)\) and leads to a composite rule with error \(C \|f'\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} n^{-1}\) (Theorem 10.1),
Trapezium rule is given by \(\frac{b-a}{2} \left( f(a) + f(b) \right)\) and leads to a composite rule with error \(C \|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])} n^{-2}\) (Theorem 10.3).

text:

Simpson’s rule: integrating the quadratic interpolant on \(\{a, \tfrac{a+b}{2}, b\}\),
Simpson’s rule is exact for cubics, and an improved error estimate using Hermite interpolation.

title: 10  Newton–Cotes quadrature
text:
10.7 Extra exercises

Exercise 10.9 (Midpoint rule) 
The midpoint rule is \(\int_a^b f \approx (b-a) f\big(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\big)\).

Show that the midpoint rule is exact for all polynomials of degree at most \(1\).
Suppose \(f \in C^2([a,b])\). Show that \[
\left| \int_a^b f - (b-a) f\big(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\big) \right| \leq \frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{24} (b-a)^3.
\]
Write down the composite midpoint rule on \(n\) subintervals of equal length and show that its error is bounded by \(\frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{24} \frac{(b-a)^3}{n^2}\). Compare with Theorem 10.3.


For 2, use Taylor’s theorem about \(m = \frac{a+b}{2}\):
\[\begin{align}
    f(x) = f(m) + f'(m)(x - m) + \frac{f''(\xi_x)}{2}(x-m)^2.
\end{align}\]


Let \(m = \frac{a+b}{2}\).

For \(f = 1\): \(\int_a^b 1 = b - a = (b-a) \cdot 1\). For \(f = x - m\): \[
\begin{align}
\int_a^b (x - m) \,\mathrm{d}x &= 0
\nonumber\\
%
&= (b-a)(m - m).
\end{align}
\]
By Taylor’s theorem, \[
\begin{align}
f(x) = f(m) + f'(m)(x-m) + \frac{f''(\xi_x)}{2} (x-m)^2
\end{align}
\] for some \(\xi_x\) between \(m\) and \(x\). Integrating and using \(\int_a^b (x - m) \,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), \[
\begin{align}
\left| \int_a^b f - (b-a) f(m) \right|
%
&= \left| \int_a^b \frac{f''(\xi_x)}{2} (x-m)^2 \,\mathrm{d}x \right| \nonumber\\
%
&\leq \frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \int_a^b (x - m)^2 \,\mathrm{d}x
\nonumber\\
%
&= \frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{2} \frac{(b-a)^3}{12}.
\end{align}
\]
With \(x_j = a + j \frac{b-a}{n}\), the composite rule is \(\frac{b-a}{n} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f\big( \frac{x_j + x_{j+1}}{2} \big)\). Applying 2 on each subinterval of length \(\frac{b-a}{n}\) and summing the \(n\) errors gives \[
\begin{align}
n \cdot \frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{24} \Big( \frac{b-a}{n} \Big)^3
%
&= \frac{\|f''\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}}{24} \frac{(b-a)^3}{n^2}.
\end{align}
\] This is the same rate \(O(n^{-2})\) as the composite trapezoid rule, but with half the constant (and one fewer function evaluation).




Exercise 10.10 (Properties of interpolatory weights) 
Let \(x_0, \dots, x_n \in [a,b]\) be distinct and let \(w_j = \int_a^b \ell_j\) be the weights in (10.2).

Show that \(\{w_j\}\) are the unique weights for which \(\sum_{j=0}^n w_j f(x_j)\) is exact for all \(f \in \mathcal P_n\).
Show that \(\sum_{j=0}^n w_j = b - a\).
Let \(\hat x_j \in [0,1]\) and let \(\hat w_j\) be the corresponding weights on \([0,1]\). Show that the nodes \(x_j = a + (b-a) \hat x_j\) on \([a,b]\) have weights \(w_j = (b-a) \hat w_j\).
Suppose the nodes are symmetric: \(x_{n-j} = a + b - x_j\) for all \(j\). Show that \(w_{n-j} = w_j\).



What happens if you apply the rule to \(f(x) = \ell_j(x)\)?
What happens if you apply the rule to \(f(x) = 1\)?
Use \(w_j = \int_a^b \ell_j\),
Show that \(\ell_{n-j}(x) = \ell_j(a + b - x)\) by checking the values of both sides at the nodes.




If \(f \in \mathcal P_n\) then \(f\) is its own interpolant, \(f = \sum_j \ell_j f(x_j)\), and so \(\int_a^b f = \sum_j w_j f(x_j)\) and the rule is exact. Conversely, if \(\sum_j w_j f(x_j)\) is exact on \(\mathcal P_n\), then applying it to \(\ell_j \in \mathcal P_n\) gives \(w_j = \int_a^b \ell_j = \sum_k w_k \ell_j(x_k) = w_j\), as required.
Apply 1 to \(f = 1\): \(b - a = \int_a^b 1 = \sum_j w_j\).
Write \(x = a + (b-a) t\). Since \(x - x_j = (b-a)(t - \hat x_j)\), we have \[
\begin{align}
\ell_j(x) &= \prod_{k \not= j} \frac{x - x_k}{x_j - x_k}
\nonumber\\
%
&= \prod_{k\not=j} \frac{t - \hat x_k}{\hat x_j - \hat x_k}
\nonumber\\
%
&= \hat \ell_j(t).
\end{align}
\] Therefore \[
\begin{align}
w_j = \int_a^b \ell_j(x) \,\mathrm{d}x = (b-a) \int_0^1 \hat\ell_j(t) \,\mathrm{d}t = (b-a) \hat w_j.
\end{align}
\]
Let \(q(x) := \ell_j(a + b - x) \in \mathcal P_n\). Then \(q(x_{n-k}) = \ell_j(x_k) = \delta_{jk}\). That is, \(q(x_k) = \delta_{k, n-j}\), so \(q = \ell_{n-j}\). Substituting \(y = a + b - x\), \[
\begin{align}
w_{n-j} &= \int_a^b \ell_j(a+b-x) \,\mathrm{d}x \nonumber\\
%
&= \int_a^b \ell_j(y) \,\mathrm{d}y \nonumber\\
%
&= w_j.
\end{align}
\]
